Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (true/false, match the columns, fill in the blanks or give reasons).

questions.q: State whether True or False. (a) Purple, red-purple and red make up an analogous colour scheme. (b) Shade is obtained by adding black to a colour. (c) A triad colour scheme is used in girls' frocks. (d) Bright red is used to denote peace.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) True. (c) False: a complementary scheme is suited to children's wear. (d) False: it denotes passion and danger.

questions.q: Match Column A with Column B. A: (1) Yellow and purple (2) Yellow, red-purple, blue-purple (3) Red, yellow, blue (4) Green, yellow-orange, red, blue-purple. B: (a) Split complementary (b) Triad (c) Tetrad (d) Complementary.
Give one word. (a) Brightness or dullness of a colour (b) Lightness or darkness of a colour (c) A lighter colour (d) A darker colour.
questions.answer: (a) Intensity. (b) Value. (c) Tint. (d) Shade or tone.

questions.q: Complete the equation. (a) Red + Blue = ____ (b) Yellow + ____ = Yellow orange (c) ____ + Green = Blue green.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: What are neutral colours, and why are they important in embroidery? Explain with an example.
questions.answer: Neutral colours are white, black, grey, brown, tan and beige. They give an effective background for bright colours and are useful when unsure of a scheme, such as white threadwork on a grey fabric.

questions.q: What are metallic colours? Name two traditional types of metallic wires used in Indian embroidery.
questions.answer: Metallic colours are the sparkle and shimmer of metal used in embroidery. Badla is plain gold or silver wire and kasab is the wire wound around a thread.

questions.q: Differentiate between warm and cool colours.
questions.answer: Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) feel warm and exciting and reduce size. Cool colours (blue, green, purple) feel peaceful and increase size.

questions.q: Define tertiary colours with an example.
questions.answer: They are formed by mixing a primary and a secondary colour in equal quantity, such as blue and green gives blue-green.

questions.q: What is the difference between a tint and a shade?
questions.answer: A tint is a lighter colour got by adding white to a hue. A shade or tone is a darker colour got by adding black.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain complementary and split complementary colour schemes (three points).
questions.answer: (i) A complementary scheme uses two colours opposite each other, such as red and green. (ii) A split complementary scheme uses one colour and the two colours on either side of its complement, such as yellow with red-purple and blue-purple. (iii) Both are bright and can be made suitable for all ages by changing the value and intensity.

questions.q: Explain the three characteristics of colour.
questions.answer: (i) Hue is the name of the colour such as red or blue. (ii) Value is its lightness or darkness (tints and shades). (iii) Intensity is its brightness or dullness.

questions.q: List the factors influencing the use of colours with examples (three points).
questions.answer: (i) Age and sex: bright colours for children and young adults. (ii) Occasion and season: cool, soft colours in summer; bright and dark colours in winter. (iii) Type of garment, profession and body structure.

questions.q: Explain the meaning of any three colours.
questions.answer: (i) Red denotes love, health and vitality (dark) or passion and danger (bright). (ii) Blue denotes calmness, sincerity and idealism. (iii) Purple denotes magnificence and royalty.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain the different colour schemes with examples.
questions.answer: (i) Monochromatic: tints and shades of one colour. (ii) Analogous: neighbouring colours, such as yellow, yellow-green and green. (iii) Complementary: opposite colours, such as red and green. (iv) Split complementary: yellow with red-purple and blue-purple. (v) Triad: three colours forming an equilateral triangle, such as red, yellow and blue. (vi) Tetrad: four colours forming a square, used in Kashida, Kantha and Chamba Rumal.
